# Concepts and type matching

A generic procedure with `[T]` accepts any type. That is often too loose: the body uses `x.name`,
but nothing stops a caller from passing an `int`. Constraints such as `[T: SomeInteger]` help, yet
the list is fixed by the language. A concept fills the gap: a constraint you write yourself, based
on the shape of a type.

This chapter builds concepts from the simple to the combined, uses them to pick overloads, and reads
error messages when a requirement is not met. Every example is tested on Nim 2.2.12.

::: {.callout-note}
## What you will be able to do

After this chapter you can write a `concept`, use it as a generic constraint, combine requirements
with `and` and `or`, use a concept to select an overload, and read the message
`concept predicate failed`.
:::

## Built-in constraints: `SomeNumber`

Nim ships with a few ready-made constraints.

```{.nim}
proc total[T: SomeNumber](xs: seq[T]): T =
  for x in xs:
    result += x

echo total(@[1, 2, 3])
echo total(@[1.5, 2.5])
```

```{.txt}
6
4.0
```

`SomeNumber` covers the numeric types. One procedure, two different types, no rewriting. Constraints
like this are useful as long as the shape you want already exists in the standard library. Once what
you need is "has a `name` field", no built-in name helps.

## Concepts: a requirement you write yourself

A concept lists its requirements as expressions that must hold for the type.

```{.nim}
type
  Named = concept x
    x.name is string

  Person = object
    name: string

  Robot = object
    name: string
    model: int

proc greet[T: Named](x: T): string =
  "Hello, " & x.name

echo greet(Person(name: "Ada"))
echo greet(Robot(name: "R2", model: 2))
```

```{.txt}
Hello, Ada
Hello, R2
```

`x.name is string` is the requirement: any type with a `name` field of type `string` matches. Note
that `Person` and `Robot` are unrelated. A concept matches the **shape**, not inheritance or a type's
name.

## Two requirements mean both must hold

Several lines inside one concept are joined with `and` implicitly.

```{.nim}
type
  Person = concept x
    x.name is string
    x.age is int

type Employee = object
  name: string
  age: int

proc show[T: Person](x: T): string =
  x.name & " is " & $x.age

echo show(Employee(name: "Ada", age: 36))
```

```{.txt}
Ada is 36
```

`Employee` matches because it satisfies both requirements. If even one fails, say `age` has type
`string`, the type is rejected.

## A concept selects which overload is used

Because a concept filters types, several procedures with the same name can coexist, each catching a
different group of types.

```{.nim}
type
  Named = concept x
    x.name is string
  Sized = concept x
    x.size is int

type
  Label = object
    name: string
  Box = object
    size: int

proc describe[T: Named](x: T): string = "named " & x.name
proc describe[T: Sized](x: T): string = "sized " & $x.size

echo describe(Label(name: "kit"))
echo describe(Box(size: 3))
```

```{.txt}
named kit
sized 3
```

`Label` matches only `Named`, `Box` only `Sized`, so the compiler is not in doubt. If one type
satisfies both, the call becomes ambiguous and must be resolved some other way. Keep concepts narrow
for that reason.

## Combining concepts with `and`

Two concepts can be joined with `and` in the constraint position.

```{.nim}
type
  Named = concept x
    x.name is string
  Aged = concept x
    x.age is int

type Employee = object
  name: string
  age: int

proc show[T: Named and Aged](x: T): string =
  x.name & " (" & $x.age & ")"

echo show(Employee(name: "Ada", age: 36))
```

```{.txt}
Ada (36)
```

`Named and Aged` requires both at once. The difference from two lines inside one concept: here `and`
joins concepts that can be reused separately.

## Combining concepts with `or`

`or` loosens the requirement: satisfying either one is enough.

```{.nim}
type
  HasName = concept x
    x.name is string
  HasSize = concept x
    x.size is int
  Describable = HasName or HasSize

proc describe[T: Describable](x: T): string =
  when x is HasName:
    "name: " & x.name
  else:
    "size: " & $x.size

type
  Label = object
    name: string
  Box = object
    size: int

echo describe(Label(name: "kit"))
echo describe(Box(size: 3))
```

```{.txt}
name: kit
size: 3
```

Since a matching type may have only one of the fields, the procedure body must check which branch
applies. `when x is HasName` picks at compile time, and each branch touches only the field it is
guaranteed to have. This pattern shows up often as soon as `or` is used.

## Reading the error: predicate failed

Calling a procedure with a type that does not meet the concept is rejected by the compiler.

```{.nim}
type
  Named = concept x
    x.name is string

proc greet[T: Named](x: T): string =
  "Hello, " & x.name

echo greet(42)
```

```{.txt}
main.nim(8, 11) Error: type mismatch
Expression: greet(42)
  [1] 42: int literal(42)

Expected one of (first mismatch at [position]):
[1] proc greet[T: Named](x: T): string
main.nim(3, 6) Named: undeclared field: 'name'
main.nim(3, 6) Named: undeclared field: '.'
main.nim(3, 6) Named: undeclared field: '.'
main.nim(3, 6) Named: expression '' has no type (or is ambiguous)
main.nim(3, 5) Named: concept predicate failed
```

Read it from the bottom. The last line, `concept predicate failed`, names the actual cause. The lines
above point at the file and line of the concept, `Named` on line 3, then detail which expression
failed. The compiler tries `x.name` on `int`, finds no `name` field, and reports it once per piece of
the expression. The message is long, but its direction is clear: inspect the concept on the line it
names.

## The limits of a concept

A concept is a matching tool, not an ordinary type. It cannot be used to declare a variable.

```{.nim}
type
  Named = concept x
    x.name is string

var value: Named
echo value
```

```{.txt}
main.nim(5, 5) Error: invalid type: 'Named' for var
```

Beyond that, matching is structural: a type that happens to have a `name` field matches too, even
when its author never intended it. A concept also does not check meaning, only shape. For a type
that truly must be listed explicitly, inheritance or `distinct` is a better fit than a concept.

## Exercises

Answers are in [Appendix A](../appendix/answers.qmd).

1. Write a concept `Sized` that requires `x.size is int`, then a procedure that prints the size for a
   type `Box`.
2. Does `type Num = object` with a `name: int` field match `Named`? Run it to prove your answer.
3. Combine two concepts with `and`, then use the result as the constraint of one procedure.
4. Explain why `var value: Named` is rejected by the compiler, then write the equivalent declaration
   using a concrete type that has a `name` field.

## Summary

- A `concept` filters types by shape, for example `x.name is string`.
- Several lines inside one concept are joined with `and` implicitly.
- `and` and `or` combine concepts; `or` forces the procedure body to branch with `when`.
- A concept can select an overload as long as each type matches only one candidate.
- A concept is not a type: `var x: Named` is rejected, and a failed match appears as
  `concept predicate failed`.
